description:
In anticipation of Nigeria’s 2027 general election, the African Studies Center (ASC) is organizing “Nigeria’s 2027 Elections and the Future of Democracy in Africa: Film Screening and Panel Discussion.” The program will examine Nigeria’s democratic journey and prospects through a screening of *MKO*, a recently released documentary about the annulment of the 1993 presidential election and the military dictatorship that followed, followed by a featured panel discussion on nearly three decades of civilian rule.

The panel will feature Nigerian-American filmmaker and journalist Ose Oyamendan, who covered the 1993 election and participated in the protests that followed the annulment of its results, along with faculty and colleagues from Political Science, the Department of Afroamerican and African Studies (DAAS), and the African Studies Center. The discussion will invite panelists to reflect on the historical significance of the 1993 election, the evolution of Nigerian democracy since the transition to civilian rule, and the opportunities and challenges ahead. A dinner for the panelists will follow the program.

*MKO* (2026)
Documentary, 108 minutes (1 hour and 48 minutes)
Director: Ose Oyamendan

*MKO*, directed by Nigerian-American filmmaker Ose Oyamendan, explores the life, political struggle, and controversial death of Moshood Kashimawo Olawale Abiola, popularly known as M. K. O. Abiola.

Chief Moshood Kashimawo Olawale Abiola, GCFR, was a Nigerian business magnate, publisher, philanthropist, and politician. In June 1993, he ran for president and won an election widely regarded as free and fair, but Nigeria’s military government annulled the results. The annulment prompted nationwide protests, the extrajudicial killing of protesters, and the detention of activists, including Abiola. He later died in military custody on July 7, 1998, under controversial circumstances. His death helped catalyze the dismantling of military rule and Nigeria’s return to civilian democratic governance.


Panel Discussion:
Ose Oyamendan, Nigerian-American journalist and filmmaker

Omolade Adunbi, ASC Director and Professor of Afroamerican and African Studies/Anthropology/Law, University of Michigan

Jenna Bednar, Professor of Political Science, University of Michigan

Adrian Deese, Assistant Professor of Afroamerican and African Studies, University of Michigan

Ji Yeon (Jean) Hong, Associate Professor of Political Science and Korea Foundation Professor of Korean Studies, University of Michigan

Bios:

Ose Oyamendan is a Nigerian-American filmmaker based between Los Angeles, Lagos, and London. His debut feature is the critically acclaimed and award-winning documentary *Aswat Acherim*, which explores unlikely war zone friendships between residents of Sderot, an Israeli village, and their neighbors in Gaza. His sophomore film, *MKO*, debuted to critical acclaim at the 2026 Sheffield International Documentary Film Festival. Since graduating with an MFA, Ose has directed a few dozen commercials, short films, and documentary films in the USA, Africa, Europe, and the Middle East. He is an award winner at Tribeca, Rome, and Houston Worldfest film festivals. His projects have been shown all over the world in theaters, on television, and on streaming platforms.

Omolade Adunbi is a political and environmental anthropologist and professor of Afroamerican and African Studies in the Department of Afroamerican and African Studies (DAAS).  His research examines the dynamics of power, natural resource extractive practices, governance, human and environmental rights, culture, transnational institutions, multinational corporations, and the postcolonial state.

Adrian M. Deese is an assistant professor of Afroamerican and African studies at the University of Michigan. He completed a PhD in religious studies at the University of Cambridge in England. His research focuses on religious diversity and interreligious dialogue in nineteenth-century West Africa.

Ji Yeon (Jean) Hong is an Associate Professor of Political Science and Korea Foundation Professor of Korean Studies. Her research centers on the political economy of authoritarianism, with a regional focus on East Asia. She is particularly interested in the institutional legacies of colonialism and authoritarian rule.

event_subtitle: "Inflammation-on-a-Chip: Redefining How We Study Immune Responses," with Laurel Hind, Ph.D.
description:
Inflammation-on-a-Chip: Redefining How We Study Immune Responses
Abstract:

The innate immune response must coordinate diverse cell populations to eliminate pathogens, heal wounds, and maintain tissue homeostasis. This coordination depends on dynamic communication between immune cells and their surrounding tissue environment, yet even subtle disruptions in these interactions can drive chronic inflammation and contribute to diseases including cancer, cardiovascular disease, fibrosis, and autoimmunity. As immunotherapies continue to transform the treatment of disease, a central challenge remains: understanding how innate immune cells integrate complex environmental cues to execute precise, context-dependent functions.

A major obstacle to answering this question has been the lack of experimental models that recapitulate the human inflammation microenvironment. Conventional in vitro systems often fail to capture the three-dimensional architecture of tissues or critical multicellular interactions that shape immune responses in vivo. In this seminar, I will present our research investigating cell-cell interactions using our “inflammation-on-a-chip” microphysiological system with a focus on critical signaling between myeloid cells, neutrophils, and the vascular endothelium.    

Bio:
Laurel Hind is an Assistant Professor in the Department of Chemical and Biological Engineering at the University of Colorado – Boulder. She received her BS in Chemical and Biological Engineering from the University of Wisconsin – Madison in 2009 and her PhD in Bioengineering from the University of Pennsylvania in 2015 before beginning her postdoc at University of Wisconsin – Madison. She joined the faculty at the University of Colorado – Boulder in January 2020. Her research group is broadly interested in using engineered devices to understand how diverse signals in the tissue microenvironment regulate the innate immune response. She received an NIGMS R35 Early Investigator MIRA award in 2021, was awarded an NSF CAREER award in 2025, and was named a CMBE Rising Star in 2025.

event_title: IES Energy Seminar Series - Planning optimization approaches for power systems under wildfire-related decision-dependent uncertainty
combined_title: IES Energy Seminar Series - Planning optimization approaches for power systems under wildfire-related decision-dependent uncertainty: Alex Moreira, LBNL
description:
Abstract: 
The interaction between power systems and wildfires can be dangerous and costly. Distribution grids can be liable for the outbreak of wildfires during extreme weather. In wildfire-prone areas, investment planning should consider the impact of operational actions on wildfire-related uncertainties affecting line failure likelihood. To address this planning exercise, we propose two decision-dependent uncertainty (DDU) aware  frameworks  to optimize the combination of upgrades to improve the system’s ability to deal with wildfires. The first one is two-stage distributionally robust planning optimization problem with DDU, where the first stage determines optimal switching actions and line investments, and the second stage evaluates the worst-case expected operational cost under a DDU framework designed to account for the endogenous impact of power-flow levels and hardening investment decisions in the line failure probabilities. The second one is a multi-horizon planning framework that integrates these timescales within a single distributionally robust stochastic optimization model to capture both long-term and short-term uncertainties. We develop an exact decomposition algorithm that produces coordinated investment and operational policies across both horizons.

Biography:
Alexandre Moreira is a research scientist in the Energy Technologies Area at Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory. His research applies mathematical programming techniques to critical questions in power systems planning, operations, and economics, with a particular focus on novel methodologies for transmission expansion planning that account for reliability and resilience. At Berkeley Lab, he leads and collaborates on projects that develop foundational modeling frameworks and tools to (i) formulate risk-based optimization and decision-making models to propose transparent, well-informed "cost vs. risk" tradeoffs for infrastructure planning, and (ii) support the valuation of emerging technologies. He holds BSc and MSc degrees from PUC-Rio, Brazil, and a PhD from Imperial College London.

event_title: EIHS Lecture: Ottoman Roots
combined_title: EIHS Lecture: Ottoman Roots: Samuel Dolbee (Vanderbilt University)
description:
Fruit trees planted in the late Ottoman Empire may have lived for over a century after the polity they grew up in disappeared from maps. Starting from these trees and their relationship to time, this presentation elucidates the relationship between fruit production and violence at the end of empire. Many who planted the trees left—or were forced to leave—and newly settled people—many of them refugees themselves—came to care for these living relics of past social worlds. Through apricots, figs, grapes, hazelnuts, olives, and pistachios, the project places displaced people and their rootedness in the face of uprooting at the center, and suggests their role in Turkey’s world-leading production of these commodities today. 

Samuel Dolbee is an environmental historian of the modern Middle East, and an assistant professor at Vanderbilt University. His first book Locusts of Power was the co-winner of the 2024 Ottoman and Turkish Studies Association Book Prize. His work has appeared in American Historical Review, Comparative Studies of Society and History, Environmental History, Journal of Global History, and Past & Present among other places. He was formerly editor-in-chief of and is currently a contributor to Ottoman History Podcast. 

This event presented by the Eisenberg Institute for Historical Studies. It is made possible in part by a generous contribution from Kenneth and Frances Aftel Eisenberg.

event_title: Gomberg's Earlier Instances of Trivalent Carbon
combined_title: Gomberg's Earlier Instances of Trivalent Carbon: Bart Kahr | NYU
description: University of Michigan chemistry professor Moses Gomberg’s 1900 revelation, “An Instance of Trivalent Carbon: Triphenylmethyl", lauded on a centennial National Historic Chemical Landmark for challenging the “prevailing belief that carbon can only have four bonds”, shifts its' place in our imaginations as the facts given here are accommodated. In 1898 Gomberg presumed that he had made a molecular complex of bromotriphenylmethane and two neutral iodine molecules. But he was mistaken. Instead, Gomberg produced a mixture ofthree persistent single crystals of the triphenylmethyl cation before he published his aforementioned, controversial paper. Trigonal carbon coordination was the crack in the valency rules that had organized chemistry prior to the invention of quantum mechanics. Gomberg did not recognize the wealth of trivalent carbon compounds he had in hand before the proposition of the radical and corresponding cation thereafter. This presentation gives a counterfactual history.

description:
University of Michigan’s Philosophy, Politics, and Economics speaker for Fall 2026 is Dart Lindsley, CEO of the work design company 11fold and host of Work for Humans. 

October 29, 2026 | Talk with Q & A 4pm - 6 pm | Reception with light refreshments from 6 pm to 7:30 pm.
FREE, but registration is required.
Rackham Assembly Hall

About Dart
Dart spent 25 years in transformation roles at Fortune 100 high-tech companies, serving as a Strategic Advisor and Head of Global Process Excellence for People Operations at Google, and previously as a Head of Business Architecture at Cisco Systems. He speaks on why we need to radically transform where we position employees in our business models — from inputs to customers. His 2024 HBR article "Reimagining Work as a Product" was nominated as best-of-issue and has gone on to multiple reprints.  Work for Humans has 200 episodes on which Dart speaks with diverse thinkers about how we might design better work. The show ranks in the top 3% among all podcasts and routinely peaks in the top 50 in the management category. Dart earned a 2024 Mira Fellowship for thinkers with radical reframes that can improve the world.  

About the Talk

Early management theorists committed a category error when they classified employees as inputs to production: assets, resources, human capital. Dart argues that error haunts work today and offers a reframe. Employees are customers. Work is a product they choose to buy with their labor. Like any subscription product, it has to be designed well enough that working customers choose to buy it each day. Building on his HBR article "Reimagining Work as a Product" (with co-author Eric Anicich), Dart shows how this reframe overturns norms, power structures, and how resources are allocated. For researchers it changes the questions, the units of analysis, the standards of evidence. He shares examples from organizations already living in the new world. He'll then use the reframe as a case study in something larger: what it takes to lead a paradigm shift, and the tools that serve anyone striving to redesign institutions to solve the problems of living and working together.

Registration required.

event_title: The Early Novel in French: Poetics of a Genre in the Making.
combined_title: The Early Novel in French: Poetics of a Genre in the Making.: A Lecture by Dr. Virginia Krause
event_subtitle: A Lecture by Dr. Virginia Krause
description:
In her upcoming talk, Virginia Krause proposes to fill in a missing chapter in our History of the Novel, which has long overlooked sixteenth-century France in its rush to identify the birth of the modern novel (for modernists) or the demise of medieval romance (for medievalists).  In the experimental fictions of mid-sixteenth-century France, ancient rhetorical culture and new print technologies converged, Krause argues, shedding new light on a rapidly evolving genre—its lifelike personas or “person-fictions”; its immersive powers over readers; and, amidst all its experimental properties and “new” technologies, the enduring place occupied by ancient rhetorical culture and medieval adventure, core principles for this genre-in-the-making.

*Biography:*

Professor of French and Francophone Studies at Brown University, Virginia Krause is the author of Witchcraft, Demonology, and Confession in Early Modern France (Cambridge, 2015) and Idle Pursuits (Delaware, 2003).  Her talk will be drawn from her new book, The Early Novel in French: Poetics of a Genre in the Making (Northwestern, forthcoming).

event_title: What’s Our Impact?: Understanding how the Arts & Humanities Matter
combined_title: What’s Our Impact?: Understanding how the Arts & Humanities Matter
description:
As people working in the humanities and the arts, we know our work matters–to our fields, to our disciplines, and to society. We have seen how the arts and humanities transform perception, provide expertise, and help people grapple with the biggest questions about what it means to be human and to live in an increasingly interconnected, yet often divided world. And, in both the arts and humanities, we know UM faculty are contributing to their disciplines in deeply meaningful ways. 

Yet, for all we know about these positive effects, arts and humanities research is often imagined to be at odds with the metric-driven language of “impact”--a term often seen as imposed from fields outside the arts and humanities. At the same time, “impact” has become the dominant framework for measuring the value of academic research. As a result, arts and humanities faculty are often called upon to describe our “impact” in ways that are legible to University leadership and funding imperatives, even as we feel uneasy about how to answer such calls in ways that are authentic to our work. How do we avoid finding ourselves outside terms that are increasingly important in the fight for the continued growth and resilience of higher education in the U.S?

“What’s Our Impact?: Understanding how the Arts & Humanities Matter” is a series of events slated for October 29 & 30 on UM’s Ann Arbor campus. A joint initiative of the UM Arts Initiative, Office of Vice President of Research (OVPR), and the Institute for Humanities, the gathering will serve arts and humanities faculty seeking more ways to discuss their work in terms that are legible within the ascendant impact paradigm, while also ensuring that those terms are authentic to our disciplines, methods, and creative practice. Through a public conversation, facilitated workshop, keynote from UM leadership, and a panel with funders, the 1.5 day long event will bring together experts–those engaging “impact” in their research, those in leadership, and those community partners with whom we work–and put them in conversation with arts and humanities leadership and researchers at the University of Michigan. In addition to allowing our communities to come together to elaborate what “impact” means on our terms, this event is also designed to help humanities and arts faculty recognize how they could become more competitive in University grant opportunities, including the Strategic Initiative Fund, the Arts Research: Incubation and Acceleration (ARIA) program, Humanities Institute Fellowship, and a range of other internal and external funding initiatives.

description:
If you are only seeing one workshop, please SIGN-IN and refresh the Sessions page! If still having issues, click this link. 
First-Year Relationship and Sexuality Talk (FYRST) is a required, in-person, and peer-facilitated workshop that came directly from feedback and listening sessions with current University of Michigan students. Our goal is to create an accessible, supportive space for student-driven conversations where all identities and experiences are welcomed and in which students can build skills and tools around identifying goals and values and then communicate effectively about those. Workshops will be offered at multiple locations and times throughout the fall semester, so please sign up for the workshop that works for you!! First-Year Relationship Sexuality Talk (FYRST) FAQ:
“How many workshops do I have to sign up for?”
You only need to sign up for 1 workshop. Attending 1 workshop will fulfill the requirement for the training. 
“I see that there is more than one session, does it matter which one I sign up for?”
It generally does not matter which workshop you sign up for. There will be a few that are designated for specific groups such as transfer students or for students looking for accommodations. If you do not fit these groups please try to save these workshops for those that do and you are free to choose among any of the other workshops. 
“Is this workshop required?”
This workshop is required for all transfer and first-year students at the University of Michigan.
“I’ve experienced harm around relationships or sexual experiences in the past and I am worried that attending this workshop may be harmful for me.” 
Our team is aware that students who are coming into the university that have experienced harm in the past. Our workshop is specifically designed to respect and validate the experiences of survivors and has been carefully constructed to avoid any specific descriptions of violence and focus instead on themes of empowerment, communication, and boundary setting. However, if you still have concerns about programming and would like to request alternative programming, please feel free to reach out at SAPAC-FYRST@umich.edu.
“What if I struggle to learn in a presentation setting? I’m an active learner.”
Our workshop is built to meet a variety of learning styles, including time for self-reflection, small group sharing, and resources to take with you to work through on your own time! This workshop is meant to be interactive and inclusive. 
“Can I request accommodations?”
We considered accessibility in creating this workshop and selecting the locations in which the workshops are help. However, we recognize many places at the University are inaccessible and we've set an * next to workshops that are on the first floor and lack stairs. These workshops also will have a presentation (other workshops we do not) and are a good fit for those who might need a large font. Please sign up for those if you feel that accommodations would assist you and reach out to SAPAC-FYRST@umich.edu if you are concerned or have questions. 
“I missed my workshop, what should I do ?”
Our team tracks attendance at each workshop by having participants swipe in with their MCard. If you are not able to attend the workshop you signed up for, our team will continue to send reminder emails until you have completed a workshop. In this case, please sign up for another workshop as soon as you can as the workshop is required and may fill up especially near the end of the semester. No need to contact SAPAC unless you are not able to reschedule. 
“I have had gender-based violence training before, can I get this requirement waived?”
As this workshop was designed with University of Michigan student feedback in mind, our workshop is unique to the UM community. Our curriculum focuses on individualized reflection and because of its interactive nature, each workshop will be unique to the people attending. Although we are excited you already have familiarity with the subject, this workshop is required for every first year and transfer student. 
“I’m a commuter/non-traditional student, do I still have to attend?"
Yes, this workshop is required for every first-year and transfer student - not only do we want every student to benefit from having this time to connect with peers, but we also want to make sure your peers benefit from what you bring to our community. If you have any concerns or questions about being able to participate, please contact SAPAC-FYRST@umich.edu.
“I still have questions! Who should I contact?"
Please contact us at SAPAC-FYRST@umich.edu.

description:
Join us for a special evening of music and storytelling celebrating the remarkable life of Ilhan New, a Korean American entrepreneur, philanthropist, and University of Michigan alum. This musical performance is presented in conjunction with the Nam Center for Korean Studies’ international conference, “Transpacific Lives in an American Century: Ilhan New as Method,” exploring New’s life and legacy across Korea and the United States.

Born in Pyongyang, New came to the United States at a young age and grew up in the Midwest. His journey took him from a Korean youth military school in Hastings, Nebraska, to Detroit and Ann Arbor, where he studied business and commerce at the University of Michigan. In 1922, he co-founded La Choy with his Michigan friend Wally Smith. Returning to Korea in 1926, he established Yuhan Corporation, a pharmaceutical company that reflected his commitment to public health and social responsibility. During and after World War II, New also contributed to Korea’s independence efforts and the rebuilding of the nation through education, philanthropy, and public health initiatives. His life offers a compelling lens through which to explore migration, identity, entrepreneurship, and the enduring connections between Korea and the United States.

Featuring original songs by Lisa Sung, this performance brings New’s extraordinary story to life through music and narrative, inviting audiences to reflect on the personal experiences and historical forces that shaped his legacy.
